_readme: The Codex's live feed. APPEND-ONLY: the caretaker adds to the front of `entries` every two days and never edits or removes what is already here. Old entries are the record; deleting one would be lying about the past.
policy: append-only · newest first · nothing is ever deleted

entries.title: CISA flags a Citrix NetScaler zero-day exploited on already-patched boxes
entries.oneline: CVE-2026-88779 crashes SAML logins for VPN and SSO gateways; federal fix deadline 7 Oct.
entries.plain: Citrix NetScaler is a box that sits at the front door of many organisations' networks, handling VPN and single sign-on logins. A newly found flaw in how it checks SAML logins — a common way of proving who you are to a company's systems — lets an attacker crash that login service with no password needed, locking staff out of remote access. The alarming part: a well-known researcher saw it being used against boxes that were already fully patched from an earlier fix, meaning that first patch didn't fully close the door. The US cyber-security agency has told its own agencies to fix it by 7 October.
entries.tech: CVE-2026-88779 (CVSS 4.0: 8.7) is a CWE-119 memory-buffer overflow in Citrix NetScaler ADC/Gateway's SAML handler (samlAction/samlIdPProfile), triggerable pre-auth to cause denial of service against the appliance's authentication service. CISA added it to KEV on 4 Oct 2026 with a 7 Oct remediation deadline under BOD 26-04. Fixed builds: 14.1-73.41+, 13.1-64.28+, FIPS 14.1-73.41/13.1-37.282+. Researcher Kevin Beaumont reported exploitation on honeypots already running the prior patch batch, suggesting the fix was incomplete; Citrix confirms DoS impact while Norway's NSM initially reported possible RCE.
entries.lands: You don't run NetScaler, but any NHS trust or supplier you work with almost certainly has one at the edge handling VPN or SSO — worth asking about during a clinical-safety or supply-chain conversation, because 'we patched it in September' is not the same as 'we're safe' here. The real lesson for your own stack: treat a patch as a hypothesis, not a guarantee, and keep watching vendor advisories after you've applied a fix — your detection plan should include 're-check after patching' as its own explicit step.
entries.toolnote: If you ever manage a NetScaler for a client, check its build number against 14.1-73.41 / 13.1-64.28 today, not after the next advisory.
entries.artcap: A patch that didn't quite close the door — exploited again on 'fixed' boxes.

entries.title: A cut subsea cable forced Philippines–Singapore traffic to reroute
entries.oneline: A reminder that every cloud API ultimately rides on physical glass under the sea.
entries.plain: The internet isn't really a cloud — it's a web of physical fibre-optic cables laid along the sea floor, and one of the cables connecting the Philippines and Singapore was cut. Telecom companies had to reroute traffic around the damage, which meant slower and patchy connections for people in the Philippines trying to reach anything hosted overseas, for a couple of days before service normalised. It's a useful, concrete reminder that even the most polished API call eventually depends on something as physical and breakable as a wire at the bottom of the ocean.
entries.tech: A subsea fibre segment on the Philippines–Singapore route (with the Philippines–Hong Kong link also affected) went offline on 2 Oct 2026, prompting Globe, PLDT and Converge ICT to reroute traffic onto alternative submarine cable systems. Telcos reported degraded, intermittent connectivity for roughly two days; full physical repair is expected to take several weeks, with traffic running on redundant links meanwhile. No concurrent hyperscaler incident was logged — AWS, GCP and Azure showed operational throughout, isolating the disruption to the physical layer.
entries.lands: None of your current infrastructure sits in that corridor, but the lesson generalises: any agent or pipeline that calls an API hosted in or routed through Asia-Pacific should have a sane timeout and retry-with-backoff, not an indefinite hang, because the failure mode here is degraded latency, not a clean error. When you document egress rules for a client's agent, note which regions its dependencies physically sit in — it's exactly the kind of question an NHS information-governance reviewer will eventually ask about resilience.
entries.toolnote: `mtr` to a dependency's hostname during a reported cable incident will show you the reroute in real time.
entries.artcap: Every API call still rides on glass under an ocean somewhere.

entries.title: Claude Code gets a plugin marketplace and backs MCP's stateless core
entries.oneline: Anthropic formalises third-party extensions and adopts MCP 2.0 — directory, auto-validation, and zero-touch OAuth included.
entries.plain: Claude Code now has a proper system for add-ons, called Plugins — a directory where anyone can submit a bundle of tools, get it checked automatically, and publish it for others to install, much like an app store. Underneath, Claude has adopted the newest version of MCP, the shared language that lets an AI assistant plug into outside tools. The new version drops the need for a server to remember who's mid-conversation, so a plugin's backend can run on ordinary, cheap, scale-to-zero hosting instead of a server that has to stay switched on all the time.
entries.tech: From 1 Oct 2026, Claude ships Plugins as the primary third-party extension mechanism: a directory submission portal with auto-validation, review status, publishing controls and post-launch analytics. Plugins can bundle MCP servers, skills, LSPs, commands, hooks and agents. Claude now supports MCP 2.0's stateless core (removing transport sessions, so servers scale via ordinary HTTP patterns) plus two extensions: MCP Apps (in-chat interactive UI) and Enterprise Managed Auth (zero-touch OAuth for enterprise users).
entries.lands: If you've built an MCP server for one of your watchers, you can now package it as a Plugin, list it in a directory instead of hand-wiring it into every client, and drop the always-on process that held conversation state — a stateless MCP server can live as a Vercel function that scales to zero between calls, exactly the hosting pattern you already use. For an NHS-facing tool, Enterprise Managed Auth is the piece worth watching: it hints at how clinical-system connectors will eventually handle sign-in without you building custom OAuth plumbing.
entries.toolnote: Check whether your existing MCP servers already implement the stateless handshake before you package them as a Plugin.
entries.artcap: The universal plug gets a directory, a store, and a stateless backend.

entries.title: Ollama ships 'decision models' that answer, not write
entries.oneline: A new /v1/systemone endpoint returns a choice, a yes/no, or a score — no essay, no API bill.
entries.plain: Normally a local language model writes you a paragraph and you have to fish the answer out of it. Ollama just added a different kind of model — a 'decision model' — that skips the essay and hands back a straight answer: which category, yes or no, or a score, each with a confidence number attached. Two small open models, Nimble and Tev1, ship as the first examples. They run entirely on your own machine, answer in well under a tenth of a second, and cost nothing per request because nothing ever leaves your computer.
entries.tech: Ollama 0.35.0 (29 Sept 2026) adds a /v1/systemone endpoint built on TypeSafe's Jev API: send a state plus up to 64 typed questions (choice, noul, score) and get back probabilities and confidence per question. Launch models: Bespoke Labs' Nimble (9B, ~9.5GB at Q8_0) and Together AI's Tev1 (4B, ~4.5GB / 0.8B, ~812MB). On 13 public benchmarks (3,880 decisions), Nimble scored 75.7% accuracy, Tev1-4B 73.3%, Tev1-0.8B 63.5%, versus Jev 1.13's 76.0%; Nimble averaged 91ms/decision on an M5 Max.
entries.lands: Your watcher agents currently burn a full LLM call just to decide something like 'is this shift covered, yes or no' or 'route to billing or technical.' Tev1-0.8B is an 812MB download — small enough to sit happily alongside your other services on the Pi 5 — and answers exactly that kind of question locally, for free, with no network round-trip. Swap any agent step that's really a classification or routing decision onto `ollama pull tev1:0.8b` first, and save your paid API calls for the steps that genuinely need reasoning or prose.
entries.toolnote: Pull the smallest Tev1 variant first and test it against a handful of your own labelled examples before trusting it in a pipeline.
entries.artcap: A new lane in the local-model runtime: decisions instead of prose.

entries.title: Cloudflare tunnels can now gate access behind an email check
entries.oneline: One flag on cloudflared adds accountless email verification to a dev tunnel URL
entries.plain: Cloudflare makes a free tool called a Tunnel that shows a website running on your own computer — like your Pi — to the internet without opening any ports on your router. From 2 October, you can add one flag to the command and force anyone who opens the link to prove their email address first, and neither you nor them need a Cloudflare account to do it. It's a quick way to share a work-in-progress page with exactly one other person, safely.
entries.tech: Cloudflare's cloudflared gained 'Protected Quick Tunnels' (2 Oct 2026): adding --allowed-mail to a tunnel run command gates the generated *.trycloudflare.com URL behind a one-time email code, restricted to listed addresses or domains, with no Cloudflare account required on either side. Shipped alongside Workers KV Instant (sub-2ms p99 reads, 250ms global replication) and Cloudflare K2, a serverless event-stream service built on R2.
entries.lands: This closes a real gap: quick tunnels were always fast but wide-open to anyone with the URL. Now a demo of an NHS-adjacent prototype, a webhook test, or a one-off dashboard for a client can be locked to their email address with one flag — no WireGuard setup, no login for them. Still not for anything persistent or sensitive; for that keep using a named tunnel behind Zero Trust or the Tailscale mesh you already run on the node.
entries.toolnote: `cloudflared tunnel --url localhost:3000 --allowed-mail you@example.com` is the whole change.
entries.artcap: A quick tunnel that now checks ID at the door.

entries.title: Claude Code now defaults to Claude Sonnet 5.5, not 5
entries.oneline: Anthropic's v2.1.287 update also adds a plugin layer and MCP sign-in prompts
entries.plain: Anthropic's command-line coding helper, Claude Code, updated on 1 October. It now defaults to a new mid-tier brain called Claude Sonnet 5.5 instead of the older Sonnet 5, at the same price. The update also added 'Claude Mods' — small plugins that change how Claude Code behaves — and fixed how it talks to MCP, the plug system that lets Claude connect to outside tools, so a connected tool can now pop up a sign-in link mid-task instead of silently failing.
entries.tech: Claude Code v2.1.287 (1 Oct 2026) ships claude-sonnet-5-5 as the default Sonnet alias on the Anthropic API (1M-token context, $2/$10 per MTok, $0.20/MTok cache reads) — Bedrock and Vertex still resolve 'sonnet' to 4.5/4.6. Adds Claude Mods (plugin-based behaviour extension), an n: filter for the background-agents view, and MCP's 2025-11-25-protocol elicitation capability, letting servers raise an in-session URL/sign-in prompt (set bareElicitationCapability:true if a server regresses).
entries.lands: If Claude Code drives work against your Pi's repos or your narrow agents, update it — the model under your fingers just changed at the default alias. Check any pinned ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL env vars before assuming you're still billed against Sonnet 5, and re-run one long agent session after upgrading before trusting it unattended overnight. The MCP sign-in prompt change also means a server you wired up for a watcher could now wait on a browser click it never needed before.
entries.toolnote: Run `claude --version` then check `/model` to confirm which Sonnet you're actually billed against.
entries.artcap: The universal plug gained a sign-in handshake.

entries.title: 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and Pi 5 jump $12.50 on memory costs
entries.oneline: Third price rise of 2026, pushing the 2GB Pi 5 to $77.50
entries.plain: Raspberry Pi boards are getting more expensive again. From 1 October, the small 2GB versions of the Pi 4 and Pi 5 went up by $12.50 each, because the memory chips inside them keep costing more to buy. The 2GB Pi 5 now costs $77.50 — more than half as much again as when it first launched. Higher-memory boards like the 8GB and 16GB versions aren't moving this time, but they already jumped earlier in the year.
entries.tech: Raspberry Pi Holdings raised prices on the 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 (to $67.50, +23%) and 2GB Raspberry Pi 5 (to $77.50, +19%) effective 1 October 2026, citing continued LPDDR4/LPDDR5 cost increases — the third hike in 2026 after rises in February and April. The 2GB Pi 5 is now 55% above its original $50 MSRP. The 1GB variants and 2GB Compute Module 4/5 are unaffected for now.
entries.lands: If you were planning a second or third node, buy before the next round — the gap between the 2GB and 4GB/8GB Pi 5 has narrowed enough that paying up for more RAM at purchase is now the better move, especially since Raspberry Pi has also started blocking after-market RAM upgrades on newer boards. For a node running several watchers plus any local model, treat 2GB as a floor, not a target.
entries.artcap: Same board, pricier memory.

entries.title: Unpatched FortiMail zero-day lets anyone write files to the device
entries.oneline: CVE-2026-104286 (CVSS 9.8) hit CISA's exploited-vulnerability list the day it was disclosed
entries.plain: Fortinet makes FortiMail, a piece of equipment lots of organisations — including ones close to the NHS — use to scan their email for threats. On 1 October, Fortinet admitted it has a serious bug: anyone on the internet, without even logging in, can trick FortiMail into saving a file somewhere it shouldn't, which can then be used to take over the whole device. Attackers are already using this. There's no proper fix yet, only a workaround, and the US government's exploited-vulnerability list flagged it the same day.
entries.tech: CVE-2026-104286 (CVSSv3 9.8) is a path-traversal plus NULL-byte neutralisation flaw (CWE-22/CWE-158) in FortiMail's GUI/IBE component, enabling unauthenticated arbitrary file write that chains to code execution. Affects FortiMail 7.2.x through 8.0.1. Fortinet published advisory FG-IR-26-175 on 1 Oct 2026; CISA added it to KEV the same day (federal remediation due 4 Oct). No patched build exists yet — only workarounds (disable IBE, or remove internet access to the management interface).
entries.lands: You almost certainly don't run FortiMail on a Pi, but the pattern matters: an unauthenticated path-traversal bug in a security appliance that's internet-facing by design. Audit anything you've exposed the same way — any admin or management interface on your node reachable without a VPN hop is one disclosure away from this exact story. If a future NHS-adjacent client runs Fortinet gear, this is a concrete, dated talking point for a threat-model conversation, not a hypothetical one.
entries.artcap: No patch yet — only a workaround and a clock.

entries.title: Anthropic's CLI now applies agents from files, like Terraform for AI
entries.oneline: ant apply plus a lockfile brings commit-and-deploy discipline to agent configs
entries.plain: Anthropic's command-line tool for Claude got a new command, ant apply, that reads a description of an agent — its tools, its memory, its environment — from a file in your repo and creates or updates it to match, the same way infrastructure tools manage cloud servers. It writes a 'lockfile' that remembers what it already built, so running it again updates the same agent instead of quietly creating duplicates. This turns 'I configured an agent by clicking around' into 'I have a file that says exactly what this agent is,' which you can commit, diff, and roll back.
entries.tech: Claude Developer Platform's ant CLI v1.30.0 adds ant apply: it reads declarative resource files (agents, environments, skills, memory stores, deployments) from a repo, prints a plan, and applies it on approval. The command writes claude-lock.json, which must be committed so subsequent runs — local or CI — mutate existing resources rather than recreating them, giving agent configuration the same commit/diff/rollback discipline as container or IaC definitions.
entries.lands: This is the missing piece between 'I built an agent in a chat UI' and 'I have a repo that defines my agents.' For your node, it means an agent's tool list, memory store, and environment variables can live in the same git repo as the rest of your Pi's config — reviewable in a diff, restorable from a commit, reproducible on a fresh SD card. Adopt it gradually: describe one existing agent as a file, run ant apply against it, commit the lockfile, and only then start managing new agents this way.
entries.artcap: Agents as files now — commit, diff, and roll back like everything else.

entries.title: DRAM's record highs carried straight into September — no reversal in sight
entries.oneline: DDR4 chips at $42.50, DDR5 kits up ~485%, and relief pushed past 2027
entries.plain: Computer memory (RAM) has been getting more expensive all year because AI data centres are buying up the same factories that make ordinary chips, and that squeeze didn't ease as summer ended. A basic DDR4 memory chip hit a record $42.50, and a 64GB DDR5 kit that used to cost a couple of hundred dollars now costs over a thousand — roughly 485% more. Trackers watching the market in September say prices are simply staying at August's record highs, not climbing further but also not coming down, and industry voices don't expect real relief before 2027 or later.
entries.tech: TrendForce's DRAMeXchange spot pricing put the mainstream DDR4 1Gx8 3200 chip at a record $42.50 and a 64GB DDR5 kit up roughly 485% to about $1,118 in August 2026. Trackers watching September pricing report no reversal — the same supply dynamics (wafer capacity reallocated to HBM for AI accelerators at Samsung/SK Hynix/Micron) that produced August's records have carried directly into the new month, with most analysts still pointing to 2027–2028 before meaningful relief.
entries.lands: Any Pi 5 upgrade, spare board, or second-hand NVMe/SSD purchase you're weighing costs meaningfully more than a year ago, and waiting isn't a strategy — prices aren't falling. If you're speccing a new node or a laptop for local model work, buy the RAM/SSD capacity you'll actually need now rather than planning a 'cheap upgrade later'; check installed memory with dmidecode before assuming you need to buy anything at all. This also raises the value of a Pi you already own: it's a comparatively cheap, fixed-cost way to keep running local models while memory prices stay high.
entries.artcap: HBM for AI accelerators is eating the wafer capacity ordinary DDR4/DDR5 used to get.

sources.label: tech-insider.org — RAM Prices 2026: DRAM Crisis Hits Record $42/Chip

entries.title: CISA lists a live MCP auth-bypass — first KEV batch built from AI plumbing
entries.oneline: A fake Bearer token was enough to reach tools behind LiteLLM's MCP gateway
entries.plain: On 2 September, the US government's list of vulnerabilities that criminals are actually using added seven new entries — and for the first time, three of them were AI infrastructure rather than classic servers. The worst for anyone running agents: a bug in LiteLLM, a popular gateway that routes requests to AI models and their tools. A made-up 'Bearer token' (normally proof you're allowed in) could trick it into letting a stranger use connected tools anyway. If you run any AI gateway that hands out tool access, this is the reminder that 'authenticated' can be a lie if nobody checks it properly.
entries.tech: CVE-2026-59822 (CVSS 8.8) is an improper-authentication flaw in LiteLLM's MCP Streamable HTTP endpoint prior to v1.84.0: a fabricated Authorization header triggers an OAuth2-passthrough fallback that swaps failed key validation for an empty UserAPIKeyAuth() object, letting unauthenticated requests list and call configured MCP tools. CISA added it to KEV on 2 Sept alongside Starlette's CVE-2026-48710 ('BadHost') and five others; three of the seven target AI/ML infrastructure specifically.
entries.lands: You almost certainly don't run LiteLLM, but the failure mode is one any home-grown MCP gateway can fall into: an auth check that fails 'open' when something upstream goes wrong. If any agent sits behind a proxy forwarding Bearer tokens to MCP servers, test what happens when the token is garbage — it should be refused, not waved through with empty credentials. Cheap, concrete fix: log every MCP tool-call with the identity it authenticated as, so a silent fallback shows up in your own logs before a stranger finds it first.
entries.artcap: Active exploitation, not theoretical risk — that's what KEV means.

sources.label: CISA — Adds Seven Known Exploited Vulnerabilities

entries.title: Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 become Anthropic's new top tier
entries.oneline: Same headline price, a quarter of the cache cost, and a quiet anti-copying lock for new accounts
entries.plain: On 1 September, Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 and a restricted twin called Mythos 5.1 — its smartest models yet for coding and long research tasks. The sticker price didn't change, but re-using saved context ('cache') got four times cheaper, which matters if you run agents that re-read the same files over and over. There's also a quieter change: brand-new API accounts can no longer edit what Claude 'thought' earlier in a conversation while keeping the transcript — a trick people used to copy how Claude reasons into cheaper rival models.
entries.tech: Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 (same weights, different safeguards) launched with a 1M-token context window and 128K max output tokens, at unchanged pricing of $10/$50 per million input/output tokens, while prompt-cache reads fell 75% to $0.25/MTok. Fable 5.1 also hardens against distillation: new API accounts can no longer edit prior-turn context while preserving Claude's thinking transcript, closing a publicly documented extraction technique.
entries.lands: If you call the Claude API from any agent, the maths just improved: repeatedly-read system prompts and tool schemas now cost a quarter as much to reuse — exactly the workload shape of a Pi-hosted watcher that re-sends the same context every cycle. No action needed on local Ollama models; this only touches API-billed work. If you ever built a pipeline that edits Claude's prior 'thinking' to steer follow-up turns, check whether your account predates September — new accounts can no longer do this.
entries.toolnote: Prompt caching is the lever — confirm your agent's system prompt is cache-eligible before assuming the discount applies.
entries.artcap: Same sticker price, cheaper reuse — the cache line moved, not the input line.

sources.label: Anthropic — Introducing Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1
Claude Platform Docs — What's new in Fable 5.1

entries.title: Claude Code locks down MCP and plugin loading after a rough patch
entries.oneline: New validation closes an OAuth redirect gap and a Windows path-traversal credential leak
entries.plain: Claude Code, the AI coding assistant many developers run in their terminal, tightened up how it loads plug-ins and connects to external tools (called MCP servers) after a run of bug reports. It now checks more carefully that a plug-in is genuinely trustworthy before running it, closes a Windows path trick that could leak login credentials, and makes the 'remote control' feature — running a coding session from your phone — recover properly if a connection drops. None of this changes what you can build; it changes how safely the tool behaves while you build it.
entries.tech: Claude Code shipped stronger gateway and plugin validation, closing an NTLM credential-leak vector via a Windows `\\?\` device-prefix path bypass, and fixed MCP OAuth redirect-URI mismatches for pre-registered clients (e.g. Slack). Remote Control sessions now reattach to existing claude.ai sessions instead of duplicating, and recover conversation history after a bridge worker restart. Added GitLab merge-request support in `--worktree`, opt-in `forward_user_identity` for per-user spend attribution, and Linux cgroup memory limits for Bash tool commands.
entries.lands: If you run Claude Code against any MCP server you didn't write yourself, this closes a real credential-leak path — pull the update before your next session touching client work. The per-user spend attribution flag (forward_user_identity) is worth switching on now if you ever bill an NHS trust or client for agent time; it gives you a free audit trail instead of building one later. Do: update Claude Code, re-check any custom MCP server's OAuth client registration.
entries.artcap: Tighter checks on what a plugin or MCP server is allowed to touch.

entries.title: CISA confirms two TrueConf Server bugs are being exploited now
entries.oneline: Missing-authentication and code-injection flaws land on the KEV list with an action-due date
entries.plain: The US government's official list of security holes that hackers are actually using right now — not just theoretical ones — added two new bugs in TrueConf Server, a video-conferencing platform. One lets an attacker skip the login screen entirely; the other lets them inject and run their own code on the server. If you or anyone you work with runs TrueConf for meetings, this is a today problem, not a someday one — the agencies that track this give a strict deadline to patch.
entries.tech: CISA added CVE-2026-72529 (TrueConf Server missing authentication for a critical function) and CVE-2026-72530 (code injection) to the KEV catalog on 20 August 2026, based on confirmed active exploitation. Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies must remediate by the published due date; private-sector and NHS-adjacent operators should treat KEV inclusion as de facto proof of in-the-wild exploitation and patch on the same timeline regardless of directive scope.
entries.lands: You don't run TrueConf, but the pattern matters: an auth-bypass-plus-code-injection pair went from disclosed to actively-exploited fast enough that CISA flagged it within days. Add TrueConf to your mental list of 'software I check against KEV before ever exposing it to the internet' — and if you ever stand up a video or comms tool for client- or NHS-facing work, check the vendor against the KEV catalog before deployment, not after. Do: bookmark cisa.gov/kev and glance at it weekly, the way you already track CVEs for your own stack.
entries.artcap: Two more entries on the queue you actually have to finish.

entries.title: Meta's first open model, Muse Glimmer, now runs everywhere in Ollama
entries.oneline: 30B multimodal agent model moves from Apple-only preview to NVIDIA, AMD and CPU support
entries.plain: Meta just released its first ever open-weight AI model, called Muse Glimmer, built to run on your own computer instead of a company's cloud. It's sized so a decent Mac or gaming PC can run it, and it can look at images as well as read text — useful for an agent that needs to check a screenshot and decide what to click. This week Ollama, the tool you use to run local models, finished adding support for it on graphics cards from NVIDIA and AMD too, not just Apple laptops, so almost anyone can now pull it down and try it.
entries.tech: Meta Superintelligence Labs' first open release, Muse Glimmer, is a 30B-parameter causal LM with a dedicated 1.8B-parameter perception encoder for native image input, Apache 2.0 licensed, 128K+ context. The Aug 10 launch supported only Ollama's MLX engine on Apple Silicon; by Aug 19 Ollama ≥0.32.8 added NVIDIA/AMD backends (18GB VRAM at Q4_K_M) plus DFlash speculative decoding, giving 1.5–1.8x speedup on Apple Silicon. Distilled from the closed Muse Spark model, benchmarked on SWE-Bench, τ³-Bench and MCP-Atlas.
entries.lands: You now have a second credible small agent model to sit next to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning — pull it on a spare machine with a real GPU (the Pi itself lacks the VRAM), point a watcher script at it, and compare tool-calling reliability before committing a workflow to one vendor. Because it's Apache 2.0, you can fine-tune and redistribute it inside an NHS-adjacent pilot without a licence review. Do: `ollama pull muse-glimmer` on your dev laptop, run one real task from HANDOFF.md through it, log the result.
entries.toolnote: Needs ~18GB VRAM or unified memory — a laptop or rented GPU, not the Pi itself.
entries.artcap: A 30B agent model, shrunk to fit a consumer GPU or a Mac.

entries.title: Claude's screen-control tool goes GA — no beta header needed
entries.oneline: Anthropic's computer use tool graduates from beta, adds batch actions and admin controls
entries.plain: Anthropic's tool that lets Claude look at a computer screen and click, type and scroll like a person has moved out of testing and is now a normal, permanent feature. It can now do several actions in one go instead of one at a time, which makes it faster for real tasks like filling in a form across multiple fields. Companies can also switch it on or off for specific staff. If you've been holding back on browser-automation agents because the tool felt experimental, that excuse is now gone.
entries.tech: The Claude API's computer use tool exits beta as computer_toolset_20260801: no beta header required, batch actions (multiple actions per turn), zoom enabled by default, and per-member configuration via the Enterprise Admin API. Existing integrations on computer_20251124 must migrate; request shape and tool handling change. Ships alongside GA Files API, Agent Skills, and a redesigned Console session viewer with sandboxed memory stores for managed agents.
entries.lands: If any of your agents drive a browser or desktop UI — checking a rota portal with no API, say — this removes the last reason to keep it in a side-project sandbox; GA means Anthropic supports it in production and won't yank it without notice. Before wiring it into anything touching NHS-adjacent systems, budget time to migrate off the old computer_20251124 shape and re-test batch-action behaviour, since a batched click sequence failing halfway through is a new failure mode your evals need to catch.
entries.artcap: Batch actions: several clicks and keystrokes issued in one turn.

entries.title: Raspberry Pi ships a $600 jig to mass-provision Compute Module 5 boards
entries.oneline: Pogo-pin fixture flashes secure boot, disk encryption and an OS onto CM5 with one clamp
entries.plain: Raspberry Pi now sells an official $600 machine that clips onto a bare Compute Module 5 board — the tiny chip-on-a-stick version of the Pi — and automatically installs an operating system, sets up security, and encrypts the storage, all by clamping a lid shut. It's built for people or small companies who need to set up many identical Pi-based devices reliably, not just one hobby project. You probably don't need one for a single Pi on your desk, but it shows Raspberry Pi is now being treated as a real production platform, not just a hobbyist toy.
entries.tech: Raspberry Pi's Compute Module 5 Programming Jig ($600) is a single-head, pogo-pin provisioning fixture: no carrier board needed, dual Ethernet (JIG + DUT ports) plus Wi-Fi, automating secure boot, full-disk encryption and bare-OS installation via the open-source rpi-sb-provisioner and rpi-image-gen tooling. Configuration happens through a localhost-only web UI reached via Raspberry Pi Connect screen sharing. Higher-throughput users run multiple jigs in parallel; per-unit programming time scales with image size, not device count.
entries.lands: This isn't for your one Pi — it's a signal for later: if a narrow-agent build of yours ever needs to become ten or a hundred identical field devices (say, a ward shift-watcher on dedicated hardware), there's now an official, secure-by-default path to mass-provision Compute Module 5s instead of hand-flashing SD cards. Worth knowing rpi-sb-provisioner and rpi-image-gen exist and are open source — you can borrow their scripted-provisioning approach for a fleet of one, long before you'd ever buy the jig itself.
entries.artcap: One clamp, one Compute Module 5, one production-ready board.

entries.title: CISA lists four more bugs already being attacked in the wild
entries.oneline: SharePoint, VMware vCenter, Windows IKE and macOS all added to the KEV catalog the same day
entries.plain: CISA — the US government's cyber-defence agency — keeps a list called the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog: software flaws that aren't just theoretical, they're already being used by real attackers right now. On 18 August 2026 it added four more: a way to trick Microsoft SharePoint into thinking you're an admin without a password, a path-traversal bug in VMware's vCenter server manager, a flaw in Windows' VPN-negotiation service, and an authentication bug in Apple's macOS. Government agencies now have a strict deadline to patch each one — and everyone else should treat that deadline as their own.
entries.tech: CISA KEV additions, 18 Aug 2026: CVE-2026-33824 (Microsoft IKE Extensions double-free), CVE-2026-55040 (SharePoint JWT auth bypass, CVSS 9.1, patched July Patch Tuesday, PoC-to-honeypot-hit within a day per Rapid7/Defused), CVE-2026-59310 (Broadcom VMware vCenter path traversal), CVE-2026-65400 (Apple macOS improper authentication). SharePoint's flaw forges a JWT to impersonate any user, including admins; Shadowserver counts 8,500+ exposed on-prem servers.
entries.lands: None of these sit on your Pi stack directly, but the pattern matters: CVE-2026-55040 went from patch to public PoC to real attacker traffic in under 24 hours. If you ever stand up SharePoint-adjacent tooling for an NHS-facing project, or manage any internet-facing admin panel, the lesson is that your patch window is now measured in hours, not weeks. Check your own exposed services against the KEV feed this week rather than 'when you get to it' — expect this exact vulnerability class to show up in NHS trust environments eventually.
entries.toolnote: Subscribe to the KEV JSON feed and diff it against your own exposed services weekly.
entries.artcap: Four fresh entries, one shared deadline: patch now, not later.

entries.title: GitHub broke for 6+ hours the same day a rival launched
entries.oneline: A global GitHub degradation and Cursor's new Origin code-host landed on the same afternoon
entries.plain: GitHub, the website almost every programmer uses to store and share code, broke for about six and a half hours on 17 August 2026. Logins failed, file downloads failed nearly half the time, and even the sign-in systems companies use to control who can access their code went down. On the very same day, a rival AI coding tool called Cursor switched on its own code-hosting service, Origin, as an alternative. It's a reminder that even giant, trusted platforms can go dark all at once — and that betting everything on one company's uptime is a real risk, not a theoretical one.
entries.tech: GitHub suffered a ~6h42m global degradation on 17 August 2026: ~20% error rates on pull requests, issues and the API, ~50% on archive/raw file downloads, plus failures in SAML, OIDC, SCIM provisioning, Team Sync and Copilot — its seventh status-page incident in fifteen days. Hours earlier, Cursor began rolling out Origin, a GitHub-style code-hosting platform (repos, PRs, code browsing, two-way GitHub sync) to paid plans, with day-one integrations for Vercel, Depot and Buildkite.
entries.lands: You run one Pi, a handful of agents and a private repo you treat as ground truth. This is the argument for a local-first git habit: your repo already lives on your Pi's disk before it ever touches a host, so an outage costs you a delayed push, not a lost afternoon. It's also a nudge to check whether your CI/CD, webhooks or deploy triggers have a single point of failure — if GitHub Actions is down, does anything on your node quietly stop updating? Worth a five-minute audit, not a platform migration.
entries.toolnote: Keep a local clone and a cron'd backup so a platform outage never touches your only copy.
entries.artcap: One company's outage, felt across a fifth of the web's front doors.

entries.title: Ollama can now run Meta's multimodal Muse Glimmer locally
entries.oneline: A 30B image-capable model and a 27B coding model join the local-model lineup this week
entries.plain: Ollama is the free tool that lets you run AI models directly on your own computer instead of paying a company to run them for you. This week it added support for two new open models: Meta's 'Muse Glimmer', a 30-billion-parameter model that can look at images as well as text, and Qwen3.8, a 27-billion-parameter model tuned for coding and long research tasks. Both are built the same clever way as recent efficient models: they only 'wake up' a small slice of their brain per word, so they run faster than their full size suggests — good news for anyone without a giant GPU.
entries.tech: Ollama shipped local support for Meta's Muse Glimmer (30B multimodal, MLX-optimized on Apple Silicon with DFlash and image input) and Qwen3.8 27B (improved instruction-following for coding, research and long-horizon agentic tasks), alongside DeepSeek Harness and Muse Code agent-harness support, across releases dated 10-16 August 2026 (Ollama v0.32.8-v0.32.13). Both target the same execution-layer niche as NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Lightning: small-active-parameter MoE models built for always-on agent loops rather than one-shot chat.
entries.lands: A 30B or 27B model at full precision won't run comfortably on a Pi 5's 8-16GB — but a quantised (Q4) version might, and this is exactly the kind of model worth testing on a rented GPU hour before deciding whether to bring it home. If you're building narrow agents that need to read a screenshot or a scanned form as well as text, Muse Glimmer's image input is the more interesting of the two for you; Qwen3.8 is the safer pick if you just want a better local coding assistant.
entries.toolnote: Test the full-size model on a rented GPU hour before committing a Pi to a quantised copy.
entries.artcap: Same trick, new names: small active parameters, big claimed capability.

entries.title: A 32GB RAM kit that cost $100 now costs $400+
entries.oneline: The AI-driven memory shortage keeps deepening, with no reversal projected before 2027-2028
entries.plain: Computer memory chips (RAM) keep getting more expensive, and it's not slowing down. A 32-gigabyte DDR5 memory kit that cost about $100 a year ago now costs well over $400, because the same factories that make ordinary RAM have been switching to make the special high-speed memory that AI data centres need instead. Analysts now expect this squeeze to last into 2027 or 2028, not months. It's part of why Raspberry Pi's own engineers have said a Pi 6 isn't coming before early 2028 — there's little point launching a new board when the memory to put in it costs twice what it used to.
entries.tech: TrendForce-reported consumer DRAM contract prices rose ~95% in Q1 2026 and a further ~63% in Q2; a 32GB DDR5-6000 kit rose from ~$100 (Sept 2025) to $400+ by August 2026 per Tom's Hardware. Citi projects enterprise 64GB DDR5 RDIMM pricing climbing from $873 (Q1 2026) to ~$1,586 by Q4 2026. Root cause: Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron (>95% of DRAM output) reallocating wafer capacity to HBM for AI accelerators; SK Hynix's CEO has said the shortage could persist beyond 2030.
entries.lands: Your Pi 5's RAM is already fixed at whatever you bought, so this doesn't touch your existing node — but it changes the maths on every future purchase: a bigger Pi, a used GPU, or a laptop upgrade for local training will all cost noticeably more than a year ago, and that gap isn't closing soon. If you've been putting off buying a 16GB Pi 5 or a memory-heavy secondhand GPU for LoRA work, this is the argument for doing it now rather than waiting for prices to 'come back down' — they aren't projected to.
entries.toolnote: Price-check any RAM-heavy purchase against TrendForce/Tom's Hardware trend data before waiting for a discount that isn't coming.
entries.artcap: Same wafers, redirected: your RAM lost the bidding war to a GPU rack.

entries.title: Samsung's HBM4 yield hits 80% — but ordinary RAM stays scarce
entries.oneline: the fastest memory chip gets easier to make; the kind in your Pi doesn't
entries.plain: Samsung just announced its newest memory chip — the super-fast kind used inside AI data centres — is now working properly about 80% of the time it's made, up from under 60% in February. That sounds like good news for everyone, but mostly isn't for you: this chip type is different from the ordinary memory that goes in your Raspberry Pi or laptop, and factories are still pouring their best capacity into it instead of ordinary memory. So the shortage pushing up Pi and laptop prices all year keeps going, even as this specific bottleneck eases somewhere else entirely.
entries.tech: Samsung's HBM4 yield reportedly reached ~80% ('golden yield') by August 2026, up from under 60% at February's mass-production start, driven by 1c DRAM base-die improvements and TC-NCF packaging progress. TrendForce (13 Aug) expects HBM to retain pricing power through 2027 as bit-shipment growth (50-60% YoY in 2027) still lags demand, while ordinary DRAM contract-price growth moderates but does not reverse — meaning LPDDR4 costs feeding Raspberry Pi's bill-of-materials stay elevated.
entries.lands: Don't wait for a Pi price cut: this yield jump is about HBM going into AI accelerators, not the LPDDR4 in your Pi 5's bill of materials, and fabs are still prioritising the higher-margin chip. If you're speccing a new node or a GPU-hour rental this quarter, budget for continued elevated memory pricing rather than a correction — TrendForce's own forecast has HBM keeping pricing power through 2027. Practically: buy RAM-heavier boards now if you genuinely need them, and lean harder on quantised models that fit in less memory rather than waiting for prices to fall.
entries.toolnote: If 16GB/8GB boards are the plan, price them this month — nothing here suggests the DRAM squeeze easing soon.
entries.artcap: HBM gets easier to make; ordinary DRAM stays the scarce resource.

entries.title: NVIDIA gives away a 30B model built for agents that never stop
entries.oneline: 3B-active MoE tuned for the tool-calling grind, not the hard thinking
entries.plain: NVIDIA gave away Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a free 30-billion-parameter model built specifically for agents that need to keep working for hours: reading files, calling tools, checking results, and trying again when something fails. Only about 3 billion of those parameters switch on for each word it produces, which is why it runs fast even though it's officially a 30B model. It's designed to be the tireless worker inside a bigger agent system — not the smartest brain, but the one that never gets tired of doing the boring repetitive steps quickly and correctly.
entries.tech: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning: 30B-parameter hybrid Mamba-2/Attention MoE with ~3B active parameters per token, native 1M-token context, NVFP4 and BF16 checkpoints, released via Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio, Exo and Unsloth. Optimised for the agent execution layer — tool calls, result validation, subagent delegation — with NVIDIA's benchmarks claiming 4x throughput and 30% lower task-completion time versus similarly-sized open models. Harness support includes OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Cline, LangChain and Claude Code.
entries.lands: This isn't a model to replace your reasoning model — it's a second, cheaper brain to sit underneath one, handling the high-volume grunt work an agent loop generates (parsing a tool result, retrying a failed call, routing a subagent) without burning tokens on a frontier model for trivial steps. At 30B/3B-active it needs a real GPU, not your Pi directly, but pairing a rented GPU-hour Nemotron instance with a Claude or local reasoning model for the hard calls is the cheapest way yet to run an always-on agent that doesn't need supervision for every step.
entries.toolnote: ollama pull nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b-a3b gets the quantised build; pair it with a reasoning model for the calls that need judgement.
entries.artcap: The execution layer: a fast, narrow model doing the loop's repetitive steps.

entries.title: CISA flags Metabase's SQL-injection zero-day as actively exploited
entries.oneline: one unauthenticated request handed attackers admin over every connected database
entries.plain: Metabase is a popular tool companies use to look at their data — and it just had a very bad bug. A single web request, needing no password at all, let an attacker become the administrator of the whole tool — including every database password Metabase had stored to connect to other systems. Attackers used this before anyone knew about it, and companies including n8n, Framework and Kilo Code have already confirmed customer data was accessed. The US government's list of vulnerabilities being actively exploited added this one on 11 August, meaning: if you or a client runs Metabase, patch today, not this week.
entries.tech: CVE-2026-72898: an unauthenticated SQL injection in Metabase's /api/session/reset_password endpoint (CVSS 3.1: 10.0), affecting self-hosted 0.58.x through 0.63.4 and Enterprise 1.58-1.63.4, grants full admin access and exposes every connected database's stored credentials. Exploited as a zero-day from ~3 August, disclosed 6 August, added to CISA's KEV catalogue 11 August alongside Cisco ASA/FTD (CVE-2026-20349). Confirmed victims: n8n, Framework, Kilo Code, Anaconda. Fix: upgrade to 0.63.5/0.62.9/0.61.11/0.60.17/0.59.21 or later; rotate every credential the instance held.
entries.lands: If you or any future NHS-adjacent client ever stands up a BI/analytics dashboard (Metabase, Superset, similar) in front of real databases, this is the lesson: that tool holds the keys to everything it connects to, so it needs the same access controls as the databases themselves — never internet-facing without an authenticating proxy in front of it. Concretely: audit anything you've deployed that stores connection strings, put it behind Tailscale rather than a public IP, and add 'does this tool hold other systems' credentials' to your own threat-modelling checklist before connecting it to anything real.
entries.toolnote: Treat any BI/analytics tool holding DB credentials as tier-1 attack surface, not an internal convenience.
entries.artcap: One unauthenticated request, admin access, every connected credential.

entries.title: GitHub, Microsoft, OpenAI, AWS and Vercel agree one agent-plugin format
entries.oneline: package a skill and its MCP server once, run it in any compatible agent
entries.plain: For the last year, if you built a useful add-on for one AI coding assistant, you had to rebuild it from scratch for every other assistant — one for GitHub's tool, a different one for Claude, another for OpenAI's. On 6 August, GitHub, Microsoft, OpenAI, Amazon, Vercel and the company behind the Cursor editor agreed on one shared format instead, with Google joining days later. Now a plugin — a bundle of instructions plus its tool connections — can be built once and installed into any of these tools, the way a phone charger now works in any phone.
entries.tech: Agent Plugins 1.0, published 6 August 2026 by GitHub, AWS, Anysphere, Microsoft, OpenAI and Vercel (Google joined as core maintainer the same day), is an open, vendor-independent packaging format bundling an agent skill with its MCP server into one installable unit, now generally available across VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, the Copilot SDK and the Copilot app. It sits on top of MCP 2026-07-28's stateless core, cutting duplicated integration work for anyone shipping a tool across multiple agent harnesses.
entries.lands: If you've built even one MCP server for your own agents, this is worth ten minutes: package it as a plugin once and it becomes usable inside GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Codex and whatever comes next, instead of you maintaining parallel wiring for each. For an operator with a Pi node and a handful of narrow agents, it lowers the cost of eventually offering a tool commercially — write the integration once and it works everywhere clients already have installed, including inside Copilot- or Claude Code-based NHS tooling.
entries.toolnote: Check whether your existing MCP servers already qualify for Plugin packaging before rebuilding anything.
entries.artcap: One plugin format, many agent clients — the universal plug gets a universal case.

entries.title: MCP's stateless spec is now live across Claude, OpenAI and WordPress
entries.oneline: The plug that connects agents to tools got simpler to host, this week
entries.plain: MCP is the standard that lets an AI agent plug into outside tools — think of it as a universal socket. <cite index="20-1,20-2">The fifth spec release, MCP 2026-07-28, moves MCP to a stateless core while hardening authorization.</cite> That sounds technical, but it means the little servers that expose your tools to an agent no longer need to hold an open connection the whole time — they can just answer one request and forget about you, like a normal website. This week that change actually started showing up inside Claude, OpenAI's tools, and even WordPress.
entries.tech: <cite index="20-13,20-14,20-15">MCP 2026-07-28 moves MCP from a bidirectional stateful protocol to a request/response model, so servers can now deploy on serverless and edge infrastructure.</cite> <cite index="72-1">OpenAI's tooling now supports the opt-in MCP 2026-07-28 protocol, including paginated discovery and non-blocking server startup.</cite> <cite index="70-3">AAIF separately shipped MCP 728, a stateless version of the protocol that no longer needs a session handshake.</cite>
entries.lands: If you're running your own MCP server off the Pi to expose a tool to Claude, the stateless model means you can drop the always-open WebSocket-style connection and serve it as a plain HTTP endpoint behind a Cloudflare Tunnel — simpler, cheaper, and easier to keep alive on a board that reboots. It's also the moment to move any exposed MCP auth over to proper OAuth 2.0/OIDC rather than a bearer token you rolled yourself.
entries.artcap: The universal plug just got a simpler socket.

entries.title: CISA adds a Metabase SQL injection to its must-patch list
entries.oneline: Three actively-exploited CVEs landed in KEV this week — one hits self-hosted dashboards
entries.plain: CISA keeps a list of security holes that criminals are already using in real attacks, and anything on that list needs fixing fast. <cite index="14-1">This week CISA added three new vulnerabilities: a Cisco firewall flaw, a Windows networking driver flaw, and a Metabase SQL injection vulnerability.</cite> Metabase is a free tool a lot of small teams and solo builders use to make dashboards from their own database — <cite index="18-1">it lets an attacker with no login inject database commands and take over the whole instance as an administrator.</cite> If you or anyone you work with runs one, patch now.
entries.tech: <cite index="14-1">CISA added CVE-2026-20349 (Cisco Secure Firewall ASA/FTD heap inspection), CVE-2026-68820 (Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock use-after-free), and CVE-2026-72898 (Metabase SQL injection) to the KEV catalog based on confirmed exploitation.</cite> <cite index="18-1">CVE-2026-72898 is rated CRITICAL with an action-due date of Aug 14, 2026, allowing an unauthenticated remote attacker to inject arbitrary SQL and gain administrator access to the instance.</cite> FCEB agencies must remediate per BOD 26-04.
entries.lands: If any narrow-agent project of yours pipes data into a self-hosted Metabase dashboard reachable from the internet, this is a today-not-this-week patch — unauthenticated SQL injection to admin takeover is about as bad as it gets for a tool sitting in front of a real database. More broadly, it's a reminder to run every self-hosted admin panel behind Tailscale rather than exposed on a port, so a KEV entry like this one is a non-event for you.
entries.artcap: One unauthenticated request, full admin — the queue you patch first.

entries.title: Meta gives away a 30B open agent model that fits one GPU
entries.oneline: Muse Glimmer is Apache-2.0, runs locally, and ships with Ollama support
entries.plain: Meta released a new AI brain called Muse Glimmer that anyone can download for free and run on their own computer, no monthly bill required. <cite index="51-1">Meta's Superintelligence Labs released Muse Glimmer on Aug. 10, a 30-billion-parameter model tuned for agent work, coding and evaluation, under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.</cite> <cite index="54-5">Meta used quantization techniques to compress the model to approximately 17 gigabytes, down from the more than 55 gigabytes a full-precision version would require.</cite> It's built to run agents — programs that plan, use tools, and finish multi-step jobs — on your own hardware instead of a company's servers.
entries.tech: <cite index="54-4">Muse Glimmer has 30 billion parameters and is optimized for agentic tasks that run locally on a device, such as schedule management, file organization, and coding.</cite> Distilled from the closed Muse Spark model via logit distillation plus SFT/RL post-training. <cite index="58-11">It is available now through Hugging Face, with support for Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, MLX, ExecuTorch, vLLM, and SGLang.</cite>
entries.lands: A Pi 5 can't run this directly — 30B at 4-bit still wants ~17-20GB on a real GPU. But it's a free, high-quality reference agent you can pull on a spare PC or a rented GPU box to test tool-calling and multi-step task patterns before you hand-carve a much smaller model for the Pi itself. Watch for distilled/quantized child models appearing on Ollama in the coming weeks — those are the ones that will actually land on your board.
entries.toolnote: Test agent behaviour on a bigger machine first, then shrink the winning design down to what the Pi can hold.
entries.artcap: A 55GB brain squeezed to 17GB — the trade every local model makes.

entries.title: RAM prices keep climbing, but the rate of increase finally slows
entries.oneline: TrendForce's Q3 forecast is still up double digits, just less brutally
entries.plain: Memory chips (RAM) are still expensive and getting more so, because factories are busy making the pricier memory that big AI data centres need instead of the ordinary kind that goes in a laptop or a small board. <cite index="32-2,32-3">The RAM shortage is still active, with suppliers reporting extremely tight conditions and retail prices for ordinary DDR4 and DDR5 kits still far above 2025 lows.</cite> The one bit of good news: <cite index="32-8">TrendForce now forecasts prices to rise 13-18% quarter over quarter in Q3 2026, slower than the extraordinary jumps earlier in the year.</cite>
entries.tech: <cite index="32-3">DRAM suppliers report extremely tight conditions in Q3 2026, with retail DDR4/DDR5 kit prices remaining far above 2025 lows.</cite> <cite index="32-8">TrendForce forecasts DRAM contract prices to rise 13-18% quarter-over-quarter in Q3 2026 — a slowdown in the rate of increase, not a reversal.</cite> CXMT's growing share (~8-9% of global DRAM) is easing supply at the margin but not restoring pre-2025 pricing.
entries.lands: This is not a Pi 5 board-price story yet, but it is an accessories story: NVMe SSD hats, extra SD/microSD stock, and any second board you're planning will keep costing more into 2027, not less. If you're budgeting a second node or a bigger SSD for the current one, buy sooner rather than waiting for a price drop that isn't coming this cycle.
entries.artcap: The same fabs, split between your board and someone's data centre.

entries.title: A worm published 2,234 poisoned packages in a single day
entries.oneline: The npm registry, not the network, is now the front door
entries.plain: On 4 August a self-spreading piece of malware got into the npm package registry — the shared cupboard almost every JavaScript project takes its ingredients from. It used stolen credentials from twelve organisations to publish over two thousand tampered versions across 444 package names, and each infected project it reached handed it more credentials to spread further. Nobody was hacked in the film sense. People simply ran the install command they run every day.
entries.tech: The keyv/cacheable compromise (tracked as the "Shai-Hulud" worm) published 2,234 malicious versions across 444 package names using credentials harvested from twelve orgs; downstream reach is reported at roughly 2bn monthly downloads. Vector: preinstall lifecycle scripts plus IDE hooks, self-propagating via exfiltrated publish tokens. It follows the axios hijack, the @redhat-cloud-services namespace push, and the TanStack pull_request_target/OIDC compromise earlier in the year.
entries.lands: Directly on anyone whose agent runs `npm install`, and on every Claude Code or CI session that installs dependencies in a fresh container — a stolen token in that container is a stolen token. The defences are unglamorous and total: commit a lockfile with integrity hashes, pin GitHub Actions by commit SHA rather than tag, set `npm config set ignore-scripts true` where you can live without lifecycle scripts, and require provenance for anything you publish yourself. On the node, this is the argument for building images from pinned digests instead of `latest`.
entries.toolnote: osv-scanner runs offline against your lockfile in seconds and is the cheapest thing on this list.
entries.artcap: supply chain — the attack nobody has to break in for

entries.title: Three more flaws confirmed as actively exploited
entries.oneline: CISA's KEV list is the only patch queue that matters tonight
entries.plain: A government body keeps a public list of security holes that criminals are provably using right now — not might use, are using. Three more went on it: one in a Cisco firewall, one in Windows, one in a data tool called Metabase. That list is the difference between a patching backlog of thousands and a to-do list of three.
entries.tech: Added 11 Aug 2026: CVE-2026-20349 (Cisco Secure Firewall), CVE-2026-68820 (Microsoft Windows), CVE-2026-72898 (Metabase SQL injection). KEV membership is evidence of exploitation, not severity — which is why it, not CVSS, should drive the queue. Pair it with EPSS for what is likely to be exploited next.
entries.lands: On how you decide what to fix first, forever. Severity scores produce a queue you will never finish; KEV produces one you can finish tonight. On the node this collapses to one habit — `unattended-upgrades` enabled on day one, so the boring 90% patches itself while you sleep, and you only make decisions about the rest.
entries.artcap: three numbers, one decision

entries.title: An incomplete patch became an authentication bypass
entries.oneline: The remote-management tool as the perfect pivot
entries.plain: A tool that IT companies use to manage thousands of their customers' computers had a hole that let attackers walk in without a password. Worse, it had been patched before — badly — so the fix was fixed and the hole stayed open. Because the tool's whole job is reaching into other people's machines, one break-in reaches everywhere it manages.
entries.tech: CVE-2026-18577 in N-able N-central: authentication bypass and account takeover from an incomplete prior patch (CVSS 8.2), added to KEV after confirmed customer compromise. Post-exploitation abuses the built-in Take Control feature to pivot into managed endpoints and plant persistence — the classic RMM blast-radius pattern.
entries.lands: On the mental model of trust, more than on your kit. Anything that manages other machines is a machine that owns them: RMM tools, your CI runner, an agent with a broad token, the SSH key that reaches every box. Inventory what has reach, give each thing the narrowest credential that still works, and treat an incomplete patch as an unpatched system until you have verified the version yourself.
entries.artcap: one foothold, then everything it manages

sources.label: The Hacker News — N-able N-central in KEV

entries.title: MCP went stateless — and that changes where agents can live
entries.oneline: The 2026-07-28 spec: request/response, real OAuth, versioned extensions
entries.plain: The universal plug between AI and other software got its biggest revision yet. The important part sounds boring: it no longer needs to hold a permanent open line. That means a tool server can now live on cheap, sleep-when-idle hosting instead of a machine that stays awake. It also grew proper sign-in, so a tool can finally know which human it is acting for.
entries.tech: MCP 2026-07-28 moves from a bidirectional stateful protocol to request/response, unblocking serverless and edge deployment; adds OAuth 2.1 / OIDC authorization, and puts Apps (embedded UI) and Tasks (long-running work) behind a versioned extensions framework. Reported ~400M monthly SDK downloads, roughly 4× year-on-year.
entries.lands: On the shape of anything you build to be called by an agent. A stateless server can be a serverless function that costs nothing when idle — but it also means your server must carry its own state and idempotency, because the protocol no longer holds the thread for you. For the node: MCP servers are now cheap enough to run one per project, and the OAuth work is what lets an agent act as you without holding your password.
entries.artcap: one socket, every tool — now without a permanent wire

entries.title: Between a third and a half of the web is already quantum-safe
entries.oneline: Hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM is now the quiet default
entries.plain: Encryption that would survive a computer that does not exist yet is already switched on for a large slice of the internet, and nobody had to do anything. Browsers and the big networks agreed a new handshake that mixes today's maths with quantum-resistant maths, so if either one breaks the other still holds. It matters now because anything recorded today can be unlocked later.
entries.tech: Hybrid key agreement (X25519 + ML-KEM, FIPS 203) is on by default across Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari and supported by the major CDNs; reported 30–50% of browser-initiated TLS 1.3 handshakes now negotiate a hybrid group. Signatures (ML-DSA, FIPS 204) lag far behind key exchange — certificate chains are the slow half of the migration.
entries.lands: On long-lived secrets more than on live traffic. Harvest-now-decrypt-later means anything you encrypt today that must still be secret in 2035 — archives, health records, family material on the seed vault — should be inventoried now. Practically: keep TLS libraries current and let the hybrid default do its work; the actual project is knowing which of your data has a long secrecy lifetime.
entries.artcap: the handshake — where the change actually landed

entries.title: Open weights caught up, and the small end got serious
entries.oneline: LFM2.5-2.6B lands; MiniMax M3 and Nemotron 3 Nano Omni top the open rankings
entries.plain: Models you can download and keep are now genuinely competitive with the ones you rent — and the tiny end of the range got good enough to matter. A 2.6-billion-dial model released this month is aimed squarely at running on small devices and doing the modest, high-volume jobs that make up most real work.
entries.tech: LiquidAI LFM2.5-2.6B (4 Aug) targets edge and lightweight-agent deployment; MiniMax M3, Grok 4.5 and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni lead current open-weight benchmark rankings. The pattern to note is efficiency-per-parameter improving faster than raw scale — quality at a given size roughly doubling year on year, which is what pulls capable inference down onto 8–16GB boards.
entries.lands: On the Pi, directly. A 2–3B model at Q4 quantisation fits comfortably in 16GB of RAM and runs on CPU at a usable few tokens a second — enough for tagging, classifying, extracting and drafting, which is the honest majority of the work you would otherwise pay per token for. Keep the rented frontier model for judgement; move the volume home.
entries.artcap: rounding the dials until the model fits the board

entries.title: The EU AI Act's transparency duties went live — the hard part slipped
entries.oneline: Article 50 applies now; Annex III high-risk pushed to Dec 2027 and Aug 2028
entries.plain: Europe's AI law reached its next milestone. The part that took effect is the honest-labelling part: if people are talking to a machine, they must be told, and synthetic images and video must be marked as such. The heavy paperwork for genuinely high-stakes uses — hiring, credit, health — was postponed by more than a year after a late amendment.
entries.tech: Article 50 transparency obligations (chatbot disclosure, AI-content marking, deepfake labelling) applied from 2 Aug 2026, as did the Commission's GPAI enforcement powers. The June 2026 Digital Omnibus amendments moved stand-alone Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I embedded systems to 2 Aug 2028. Extraterritorial where the output is used in the EU.
entries.lands: On anything you ship that talks to people. Labelling is now a build requirement, not a courtesy: say plainly that a bot is a bot, and mark generated media. The delay is breathing room, not a reprieve — if a project of yours ever touches recruitment, credit or clinical decisions, the compliance work is the product, and starting it in 2027 will be starting it late.

entries.title: The AI shortage is a packaging shortage
entries.oneline: CoWoS fully booked for 2026; HBM3E sold out, HBM4 ramping
entries.plain: Everyone assumes the scarce thing in AI is the chip. It is not — it is the step where the chip and its memory are glued together onto one slab. That capacity is sold out for the year despite being roughly quadrupled since 2024, and a handful of companies have booked almost all of it. This is the physical reason your model costs what it costs.
entries.tech: TSMC CoWoS is reported fully booked (both -S and -L) against ~1.0M wafers of 2026 demand, up from ~370k in 2024, with monthly capacity ramping from ~75–80k toward 120–130k WPM by year end; NVIDIA holds roughly 60% and the top three over 85%. HBM3E is sold out for 2026 with HBM4 ramping. Advanced packaging, not lithography or logic dies, was the binding constraint through 2025 and is projected to stay tight.
entries.lands: On price and availability, which is to say on every decision you make about renting versus owning. It explains why inference prices fall in steps rather than smoothly, why GPU rental queues exist, and why export controls target packaging and HBM rather than just the chips. It is also the strongest argument for the local-first habit: a model that runs on your own board is immune to somebody else's allocation meeting.

entries.title: No Pi 6 before 2028 — your board is the flagship for years
entries.oneline: Engineers confirm the timeline; Pi 5 stays the platform
entries.plain: The people who build the Raspberry Pi have said the next generation is unlikely before early 2028, and that when it comes it will be a faster version of the same idea rather than a different machine. For anyone buying now, that is the best possible news: the board on your desk is not about to be superseded, and everything you learn on it keeps paying out.
entries.tech: Raspberry Pi engineers confirmed in an AMA that Pi 6 is unlikely before early 2028, citing development timelines and component supply; improvements are expected to be CPU and IO performance rather than new capability classes such as an on-board AI accelerator. The Pi 500+ shipped in the current generation. Pi 5 plus CM4/CM5 remain the platform: quad-core 64-bit, PCIe, NVMe boot.
entries.lands: On whether to invest in this board or wait for the next. Wait for nothing — an 18-month-plus runway means the NVMe spine, the Hailo accelerator and every graft on the synthesis bench stay current for the whole time you would take to build them anyway. It also confirms the honest limit: no built-in AI accelerator is coming, so LLM work on the Pi stays CPU-and-RAM-bound by design.

entries.title: Sleep-when-idle hosting stops being a compromise
entries.oneline: Stateless protocols let the cheap runtime carry real work
entries.plain: For years the rule was simple: anything that had to hold a conversation open needed a machine that never sleeps, and that costs money every hour whether or not anyone calls. As the protocols around agents drop that requirement, the cheap option — code that wakes on a request and vanishes after — becomes viable for work it previously could not touch.
entries.tech: The move to request/response semantics (as in the MCP 2026-07-28 spec) removes the long-lived-connection requirement that forced tool servers onto persistent hosts. Consequence: serverless functions and edge isolates become valid targets, at the cost of pushing state, idempotency and replay handling into your own design. The 10-second and CPU-time walls still apply, so long jobs still need a queue plus a worker.
entries.lands: On where each piece of your estate should live, and it is not one answer. Bursty, short, public-facing work belongs on serverless or the edge, where idle costs nothing. Long jobs, schedules, watchers and anything holding state belong on the node, where a wall-clock hour is free. The skill is drawing that line deliberately instead of defaulting to whatever the tutorial used.
